book: 050 - Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_

chapters.relation: Six essays on friendship in the Facebook age. Tedesco asks whether the low-demand 'Facebook friendship' can reconcile the utilitarian demand for impartiality (Mill, Railton, Kagan) with the partiality of real friends, and concludes Facebook ties are only supplementary to relationships built elsewhere. Hamington surveys a hundred users and argues in Noddings's care-ethics terms that Facebook's information transfer makes caring possible (knowledge of the concrete other is necessary for care), though it also makes dropping a student over one racist comment effortless. Bloor reads Facebook through Heidegger's technological nihilism and the anonymous 'one', warning that speed of exchange erodes Aristotle's few deep, morally formative friendships, while Briggle's farewell letter to Facebook judges the site by Ivan Illich's convivial-tool criteria and Cuonzo recasts pokes and virtual gifts as efficient successors to primate grooming; Lattimore applies Bakhtin's 'excess of seeing' to how viewers 'consummate' other users' self-presentations.

Fairweather and Halpern defend status updates against the vanity charge using Hume's 'natural sympathy': ambient awareness of hundreds of News Feed lives exercises the fellow-feeling from which Humean moral standards grow, and Facebook's non-overlapping friend lists remove the dominance hierarchies of face-to-face groups. Butera uses Baudrillard's promiscuous 'ecstasy of communication' to read friending as gatekeeper, the status update as moderator of an avatar-self, and the News Feed as a synthesizer that lets users censor encounters, asking with Kierkegaard whether this control forecloses the openness to interruption that makes life meaningful. Doyle and Fraser stage Foucault against Habermas over the MI6 chief's wife's exposed profile, Facebook's Beacon advertising surveillance, and Iran's Twitter revolution: the same diffuse, productive power that lets citizens watch institutions back makes narcissistic self-disclosure ever more available for categorization and control. Bar-Tura's account of organizing Jewish-Muslim teen bowling nights tests Habermas's ideal speech situation and concludes that wall-to-wall interaction must become face-to-face meetings to build real solidarity.

Scholz completes his 'playground and factory' argument: user translations, photos and profiles are unpaid digital labor locked inside a walled garden whose data trails are sold to marketers and governments, even as the same platform hosts a genuine power to act together. Morgan and Clulow frame activism with the Communist Manifesto's class struggle, staging fictional discussion-board posts from Engels, Luxemburg and Chomsky that update the proletariat into the internet-era 'iProles', then show Facebook's ease breeding slacktivism, from the '1,000,000 For Obama To Grow An Afro!' group dwarfing real causes to the platform itself banning a father's 'Justice for Francesca Bimpson' page. Muhr and Pedersen use Zizek's interpassivity to argue the Facebook profile is a surrogate self that enjoys, believes and mourns on our behalf, like canned laughter or a Tibetan prayer wheel, deferring the social duty to be authentic while the site quietly installs its own ideology of relentlessly interesting happiness.

holes.name: Conviviality (Illich's convivial tools)
holes.what: Ivan Illich's ideal of autonomous, creative intercourse among persons, served by tools anyone can use for self-chosen ends without imposed obligations or certification.
holes.why: Chapter 14 ('Dear Facebook') evaluates Facebook entirely by Illich's convivial-tool criteria and finds its structure channels users into reluctant exhibitionism and distraction instead of conviviality.

holes.name: The Medium Is the Message (McLuhan)
holes.what: Marshall McLuhan's thesis that a medium's form or structure, not the content it carries, is what actually reshapes society and human relations.
holes.why: Chapter 14 argues Facebook's structure, a placeless many-to-many mass medium rather than a channel, is what steers users away from conviviality regardless of the content they post.

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian theorist of dialogism whose 'excess of seeing' names how a viewer perceives and completes another person in ways the person acting cannot see themselves.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses Bakhtin's excess of seeing to explain how Facebook viewers 'consummate' students' and friends' profiles from outside, and how gazing at each other's pages reflects different worlds.

holes.name: Gossip Theory of Language Evolution (Dunbar)
holes.what: Robin Dunbar's hypothesis that human language evolved to service social alliances in large groups, replacing the grooming primates use to bond.
holes.why: Chapter 15 models Facebook status updates, pokes and virtual gifts as the newest efficient replacement for grooming-based social bonding, on a par with the original leap to speech.

holes.name: The Ecstasy of Communication (Baudrillard)
holes.what: Baudrillard's account of the obscene promiscuity of networked communication, in which endless exchange exterminates the interstitial space sociality requires.
holes.why: Chapter 18 builds its whole gatekeeper-moderator-synthesizer analysis of friending, status updates and the News Feed around Baudrillard's promiscuity of networks and the fate of interstitial space, which the simulacra slug does not capture.

holes.name: Slavoj Žižek
holes.what: Slovenian Lacanian philosopher of ideology, the symbolic order, and how subjects enjoy and believe through externalized substitutes.
holes.why: Chapter 23 ('Faking It on Facebook') is built entirely on Žižek's work: canned laughter, weepers, the Tamagotchi, toilets, and the symbolic order all structure its account of the Facebook self.

holes.name: Interpassivity
holes.what: Žižek's concept of interactivity's uncanny double: deferring one's own passivity, being-affected, enjoyment and belief onto an object that undergoes them on one's behalf.
holes.why: Chapter 23 argues the Facebook profile is an interpassive medium that enjoys, believes in causes, and mourns for its user, deferring the duty to live authentically offline.
